{{Short description|Theorem about the Euclidean algorithm}}

'''Lamé's Theorem''' is the result of [[Gabriel Lamé]]'s analysis of the complexity of the [[Euclidean algorithm]]. Using [[Fibonacci sequence|Fibonacci numbers]], he proved in 1844<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lamé |first=Gabriel |year=1844 |title=Note sur la limite du nombre des divisions dans la recherche du plus grand commun diviseur entre deux nombres entiers |journal=Comptes rendus des séances de l'Académie des Sciences |language=French |volume=19 |pages=867–870}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Shallit |first=Jeffrey |date=1994-11-01 |title=Origins of the analysis of the Euclidean algorithm |journal=Historia Mathematica |language=en |volume=21 |issue=4 |pages=401–419 |doi=10.1006/hmat.1994.1031 |issn=0315-0860|doi-access=free }}</ref> that when looking for the [[greatest common divisor]] (GCD) of two [[integer]]s ''a'' and ''b'', the algorithm finishes in at most 5''k'' steps, where ''k'' is the number of digits (decimal) of ''b''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Lamé's Theorem |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ |access-date=2023-05-09 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Lame's Theorem - First Application of Fibonacci Numbers |url=https://www.cut-the-knot.org/blue/LamesTheorem.shtml |access-date=2023-05-09 |website=www.cut-the-knot.org}}</ref>

== Statement ==
The number of division steps in the Euclidean algorithm with entries <math>u\,\!</math> and <math>v\,\!</math> is less than <math>5</math> times the number of decimal digits of <math>\min(u,v)\,\!</math>.

== Proof ==
Let <math>u>v</math> be two positive integers.      Applying to them the [[Euclidean algorithm]] provides two sequences <math>(q_1,\ldots, q_{n})</math> and <math>(v_2,\ldots, v_{n})</math> of positive integers such that, setting <math>v_0=u,</math> <math>v_1=v</math> and <math>v_{n+1}=0,</math> one has
:<math>v_{i-1}=q_iv_i +v_{i+1}</math>
for <math>i=1,\ldots, n,</math> and
:<math>u>v>v_2>\cdots >v_{n}>0.</math>
The number {{mvar|n}} is called the ''number of steps'' of the Euclidean algorithm, since it is the number of [[Euclidean division]]s that are performed.

The [[Fibonacci number]]s are defined by <math>F_0=0,</math> <math>F_1=1,</math> and 
:<math>F_{n+1}=F_n+F_{n-1}</math>
for <math>n>0.</math>

The above relations show that <math>v_{n}\ge 1=F_2,</math> and <math>v_{n-1}\ge 2=F_3.</math> By [[Mathematical induction|induction]],
:<math>\begin{align}
v_{n-i-1}&=q_{n-i}v_{n-i}+v_{n-i+1}\\
 &\ge v_{n-i}+v_{n-i+1}\\
 &\ge F_{i+2}+F_{i+1} =F_{i+3}.
\end{align}</math>
So, if the Euclidean algorithm requires {{mvar|n}} steps, one has <math>v\ge F_{n+1}.</math>

One has <math>F_{k}\ge \varphi^{k-2}</math> for every integer <math>k>2</math>, where <math display=inline>\varphi=\frac {1+\sqrt 5}2</math> is the [[Golden ratio]]. This can be proved by induction, starting with <math>F_2 =\varphi^0=1,</math> <math>F_3=2> \varphi, </math> and continuing by using that <math>\varphi^2=\varphi +1:</math>
:<math>\begin{align}
F_{k+1}&=F_k+F_{k-1}\\
&\ge \varphi^{k-2}+\varphi^{k-3}\\
&=\varphi^{k-3}(1+\varphi)\\
&=\varphi^{k-1}.
\end{align}</math>

So, if {{mvar|n}} is the number of steps of the Euclidean algorithm, one has 
: <math>v\ge \varphi^{n-1},</math>
and thus
:<math>n-1 \le \frac {\log_{10} v}{\log_{10} \varphi}< 5\log_{10} v,</math>
using <math display=inline>\frac 1{\log_{10} \varphi}<5.</math>

If {{mvar|k}} is the number of [[decimal digit]]s of <math>v</math>, one has <math>v<10^k</math> and <math>\log_{10} v<k.</math>
So,
:<math>n-1<5k,</math>
and, as both members of the inequality are integers,
:<math>n\le 5k,</math>
which is exactly what Lamé's theorem asserts.

As a side result of this proof, one gets that the pairs of integers <math>(u,v)</math> that give the maximum number of steps of the Euclidean algorithm (for a given size of <math>v</math>) are the pairs of consecutive Fibonacci numbers.
